```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2,
                      dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

mirtverse sits on top of [mirt](https://philchalmers.github.io/mirt/). mirt does the
estimation; mirtverse helps you choose a model, read the results, make figures and
share them. Every mirtverse function takes an ordinary mirt model, so you can mix the
two packages freely.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(mirtverse)
```

## 1. Let mirtverse pick a model

`select_model()` fits a set of candidate models and recommends one. For dichotomous
items it compares the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models; for polytomous items the partial
credit, generalized partial credit and graded response models.

```{r}
data <- expand.table(LSAT7)
sel <- select_model(data, verbose = FALSE)
sel
```

```{r, fig.height = 2.6}
autoplot(sel)
```

The recommended model is an ordinary mirt object:

```{r}
mod <- sel$best
```

## 2. Read the results in plain language

```{r}
interpret(mod)
```

`interpret_prompt(mod)` packs the same results into a prompt you can paste into an
AI assistant to draft a longer narrative. Nothing is sent anywhere.

## 3. Tidy outputs

`tidy()`, `glance()` and `augment()` return data frames that work with dplyr,
gt, flextable or any other table package.

```{r}
tidy(mod)
glance(mod)
head(augment(mod))
item_table(mod)
```

## 4. Graphics

All graphics are ggplot2 objects, so you can change themes, labels and colours as
usual.

```{r}
gg_trace(mod)
gg_info(mod)
```

```{r}
science <- mirt(Science, 1, verbose = FALSE)
gg_wright(science)
gg_q3(science)
```

`autoplot(mod, type)` gives you every plot from one function:
`"trace"`, `"expected"`, `"info"`, `"iteminfo"`, `"se"`, `"wright"`, `"itemfit"`,
`"q3"` and `"scores"`.

## 5. Item health cards

A one-page summary per item for review meetings, with a traffic-light status.

```{r, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 6.5}
item_card(science, "Work")
```

`item_cards(mod, file = "cards.html")` writes cards for every item into one page.

## 6. One-call report

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mv_report(sel, file = "lsat7-report.html")
```

The report is a single HTML file with the model comparison, the interpretation,
tables, graphics, a sum-score conversion table, item health cards, and the R code to
reproduce everything.

## 7. Share the results with a dashboard

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mv_dashboard(mod, title = "LSAT7 results")
export_dashboard(mod, "lsat7-dashboard.html", format = "html")
```

A dashboard lets people who do not use R explore the results: the summary,
the item table with health cards, item curves with an ability slider and
more. Save it as one HTML file to email, or as a Shiny app to host. See
[Sharing results with a dashboard](dashboards.html).

## 8. Prefer clicking, or describing the analysis in words?

```{r, eval = FALSE}
launch_workbench()
mv_ask("fit a 2PL, check DIF by gender and make a report", data = mydata)
```

The workbench is a point-and-click app that writes the R code for you (see
`vignette("workbench")`). `mv_ask()` turns a plain-language request into a
complete, tested script (see the [mv_ask() guide](mv-ask-guide.html)).

## 9. Teaching IRT?

```{r, eval = FALSE}
run_lab("model-choice")
```

mirtverse includes interactive labs for measurement courses. Students fit live
models and make real testing decisions, from choosing a model to advising a
certification board, with feedback on every choice. See
[Learn IRT by doing](labs.html).
